title: Netherlands New Guinea
capsule: Netherlands New Guinea (Nederlands Nieuw-Guinea) was the western half of the island of New Guinea, retained by the Netherlands as a separate territory when Indonesian sovereignty over the Dutch East Indies was recognized in 1949. The Dutch justified their continued administration on the grounds that the Papuan population was ethnically and culturally distinct from Indonesia and deserved separate self-determination, initiating a Papuan Council in 1961 as a step toward independence. Indonesia disputed this claim and launched an armed infiltration campaign (Operation Trikora, 1961–1962); under US pressure the Netherlands transferred the territory to temporary UN administration (UNTEA) in October 1962, and it was handed to Indonesia as Irian Barat (West Irian) in May 1963. A contested "Act of Free Choice" in 1969 — in which 1,025 hand-picked representatives, not the general population, voted for integration — formalized Indonesian sovereignty.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Territorial boundary is clearly defined — the 141st meridian dividing Dutch from Australian New Guinea — and well documented in international agreements; the political status dispute does not affect the geographic boundary.
